plotnine is the grammar of graphics in Python: you build a plot by declaring
mappings from data to visual properties, then layering on geometric objects.

## 2a. Your first plot

Everything below runs in your browser. Press ▶ Run to execute a cell, and
edit the code freely — you can't break anything.

Our data is life expectancy, population and wealth (GDP per person) for
52 African countries in 2007, from [Gapminder](https://www.gapminder.org/).

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_0
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

africa_2007 = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa_2007.csv")
africa_2007.head()
```

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [gap_1, gap_2, gap_3, gap_4]
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

africa_2007 = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa_2007.csv")
```

A plotnine plot starts with `ggplot()`: the data, and the **mappings**
from columns to visual properties, written inside `aes()`. Then you add a
**layer** that draws something: here, a point for each row.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_1
#| autorun: true
(
    ggplot(africa_2007, aes(x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_point()
)
```

Two mappings:

1. `gdpPercap` → x position
2. `lifeExp` → y position

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Swap `x` and `y` and run the code again. The data is the same; only the
mapping changed.
:::

## 2b. More mappings

Position is not the only visual property. Here, `region` also maps to
colour:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_2
(
    ggplot(africa_2007, aes(x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_point(aes(color="region"))
)
```

Mappings can go in `ggplot()`, where every layer uses them, or in a
layer's own `aes()`, where only that layer uses them.

Population (`pop`) maps to the size of each point the same way:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_3
#| autorun: true
(
    ggplot(africa_2007, aes(x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_point(aes(color="region", size="pop"))
)
```

Now map a *number* to colour. Fill in `lifeExp`:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_4
(
    ggplot(africa_2007, aes(x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_point(aes(color=___), size=3)
)
```

::: {.solution exercise="gap_4"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_4
#| solution: true
(
    ggplot(africa_2007, aes(x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_point(aes(color="lifeExp"), size=3)
)
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## What changed?

Compare the colour legend with the one for `region`. Why is it different?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

`region` is **text**: a handful of separate categories, so it maps to
separate, distinct colours. `lifeExp` is a **number**: values that run
continuously from low to high, so it maps to a continuous colour gradient.

The kind of data decides the kind of mapping. You will use this in 2f.

Notice too that `size=3` is outside `aes()`. Inside `aes()`, a value
comes *from the data*; outside, it is a fixed setting for every point.
:::

## 2c. Layers

Life expectancy over time, for four East African countries:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: layers_0
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

africa_history = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa.csv")
ea_countries = ["Kenya", "Rwanda", "Tanzania", "Uganda"]
east_africa = africa_history.query("country in @ea_countries")
east_africa.head()
```

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [layers_1, layers_2, parsons, facet_1]
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

africa_history = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa.csv")
east_africa = africa_history[
    africa_history.country.isin(["Kenya", "Rwanda", "Tanzania", "Uganda"])
]
```

Let's draw a line through the points:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: layers_1
(
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line()
)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## What went wrong?

This isn't four lines. Why?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Nothing told plotnine that the rows belong to four different countries.
So it drew *one* line through every point from left to right, zigzagging
between countries within each year.
:::

The `group` mapping says which rows belong to the same line. Group by
country, then add a second layer: points coloured by country.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: layers_2
(
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line(aes(group=___), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="country"))
)
```

::: {.hint exercise="layers_2"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Each line is one country.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="layers_2"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: layers_2
#| solution: true
(
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="country"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="country"))
)
```
:::
:::

Layers are drawn in the order you add them, so the points sit on top of
the lines. Swap the two layers and run it again to see the difference.

The steep fall and recovery is Rwanda, around the time of the 1994
genocide.

## 2d. Put it in order

Rearrange these lines to reproduce the plot below. One line is not needed.
Cut and paste lines within the editor to reorder them.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

africa_history = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa.csv")
east_africa = africa_history[
    africa_history.country.isin(["Kenya", "Rwanda", "Tanzania", "Uganda"])
]
(
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="country"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="country"))
    + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)", color="Country")
)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: parsons
    + facet_wrap("region")
    + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)", color="Country")
    + geom_point(aes(color="country"))
)
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
(
    + geom_line(aes(group="country"), color="grey")
```

::: {.hint exercise="parsons"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Start with `ggplot()`, then add layers in drawing order. The target has a
single panel.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="parsons"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: parsons
#| solution: true
(
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="country"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="country"))
    + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)", color="Country")
)
```
:::
:::

## 2e. Small multiples

Now all 52 countries, one line each. With 52 lines in a single panel the
plot is hard to read, so `facet_wrap()` splits it into one small panel per
region. Delete the last line to see the single-panel version.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: facet_1
#| autorun: true
(
    ggplot(africa_history, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="country"), color="grey")
    + facet_wrap("region")
)
```

Faceting is a mapping too: `region` → panel.

::: {.callout-important}
## What do you see?

Which region's story was hidden in the single panel?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

**Southern Africa.** Life expectancy rose steadily to 58–64 years around
1990, then fell by 9–19 years by 2007: Swaziland went from 58.5 to 39.6.
This was the HIV/AIDS epidemic. In the single panel, those five lines
were buried among 47 others.
:::

## 2f. Discovery: the census data

Back to the table from Part 1. Its numbers were wrong, but they didn't
*look* wrong: they were plausible, well formatted numbers in neat rows.
Spotting the problem meant reading pairs of numbers and doing arithmetic
in your head.

A plot can do that work for you. Let's see whether one would have caught
the error.

### The data

`census_long.csv` holds each tribe's population in the 2014 and 2024
censuses, in two versions: `bad` (the provisional report) and `good` (the
corrected final report).

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_0
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

census = pd.read_csv("data/census_long.csv")

# List tribes from smallest to largest (corrected 2024 figures)
tribe_order = (
    census.query("version == 'good' and year == 2024")
    .sort_values("population")
    .tribe
)
census["tribe"] = pd.Categorical(census.tribe, categories=tribe_order)

# A year is a label here, not a quantity
census["year"] = census.year.astype(str)

# "Other tribes" is ~8 million people and would squash everyone else
census = census[census.tribe != "Other tribes"]

provisional = census[census.version == "bad"]
provisional.head()
```

Two of those preparation steps are already mapping decisions:

- **Year as text.** A number maps to a *continuous* colour gradient; a
  label maps to *distinct* colours. We want two clearly different colours.
- **Dropping "Other tribes".** Choosing what *not* to show is part of the
  design.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [census_1, census_2, census_3]
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

census = pd.read_csv("data/census_long.csv")
tribe_order = (
    census.query("version == 'good' and year == 2024")
    .sort_values("population")
    .tribe
)
census["tribe"] = pd.Categorical(census.tribe, categories=tribe_order)
census["year"] = census.year.astype(str)
census = census[census.tribe != "Other tribes"]
provisional = census[census.version == "bad"]
```

### Step 1: Points and lines

Map `population` to x position, `tribe` to y position and `year` to
colour. Then add a line from each tribe's 2014 point to its 2024 point:
`group` tells plotnine which points belong to the same line.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_1
(
    ggplot(provisional, aes(x=___, y=___))
    + geom_line(aes(group=___), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color=___), size=3)
)
```

::: {.hint exercise="census_1"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Column names go in quotes: `x="population"`. Each line joins the two
points for one tribe.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="census_1"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_1
#| solution: true
(
    ggplot(provisional, aes(x="population", y="tribe"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="tribe"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="year"), size=3)
)
```
:::
:::

The line comes *before* the points so that the points are drawn on top.
Layers are drawn in the order you add them.

::: {.callout-important}
## What do you see?

Across all these tribes, Uganda's population grew by about a quarter
between 2014 and 2024. Look at the length and the direction of each line.
Which tribes don't fit?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- **Bagisu** and **Acholi** go *backwards*: their populations shrank in
  ten years in which the country grew by 9 million people.
- **Bakiga** and **Langi** have far longer lines than tribes of similar
  size. Bakiga doubled.

These four tribes had their 2014 figures swapped with each other.
:::

### Step 2: Compare with the corrected figures

Now plot both versions side by side. `census` holds the `bad` and `good`
rows; split them into panels with `facet_wrap()`.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_2
(
    ggplot(census, aes(x="population", y="tribe"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="tribe"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="year"), size=3)
    + facet_wrap(___)
)
```

::: {.hint exercise="census_2"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Which column says whether a row is from the provisional or the corrected
report?
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="census_2"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_2
#| solution: true
(
    ggplot(census, aes(x="population", y="tribe"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="tribe"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="year"), size=3)
    + facet_wrap("version")
)
```
:::
:::

In the corrected figures every tribe grows, and by similar proportions.

### Step 3: Look closer (optional)

This step is optional: skip it if time is short. The four swapped tribes
jump out. Are they the only errors? Compare the two
panels row by row — the plot is yours to change. Try zooming in on the
smaller tribes.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_3
small_tribes = ["Lugbara", "Banyoro", "Alur", "Bakonzo", "Batoro", "Bafumbira"]
small = census.query("tribe in @small_tribes")

(
    ggplot(small, aes(x="population", y="tribe"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="tribe"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="year"), size=3)
    + facet_wrap("version")
    + scale_x_continuous(labels=lambda s: [f"{x/1e6:.1f}M" for x in s])
)
```

The last line changes the *labels* on the x-axis (1,200,000 → 1.2M), not
the mapping itself.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

**Banyoro**, **Alur** and **Bakonzo** also had their 2014 figures swapped,
in a smaller cycle: Banyoro got Alur's figure, Alur got Bakonzo's and
Bakonzo got Banyoro's. In the corrected figures the typical (median) tribe
grew by about 27%. In the provisional figures, Bakonzo grew by 14%, Alur by
35% and Banyoro by 39%, so each is 8–13 percentage points from 27%. The big
four are 36–73 points away: Bagisu −12%, Acholi −9%, Langi +64% and Bakiga
+100%. The smaller tribes are close in size, so their error is subtle.
:::

### Why the plot worked

The table showed each population as **text in a cell**. To see growth,
you had to read two numbers and subtract.

The plot maps the change to the **length and direction of a line**, and
the population to a **position** on a shared axis. Position and length are
the two properties people read most accurately, so you see the change
without reading a single number.

The data didn't change. The mapping did.

## Other ways to show the change

The dumbbell chart is one mapping among many. Each plot below shows the
same census data with a different mapping. Run them, then change the code.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [alt_bars, alt_box, alt_lollipop, alt_index]
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

census = pd.read_csv("data/census_long.csv")
census = census[census.tribe != "Other tribes"]
tribe_order = (
    census.query("version == 'good' and year == 2024")
    .sort_values("population")
    .tribe
)
census["tribe"] = pd.Categorical(census.tribe, categories=tribe_order)

# One row per tribe and version, with the growth between the two censuses
wide = census.pivot_table(
    index=["tribe", "version"],
    columns="year",
    values="population",
    observed=True,
).reset_index()
wide.columns = ["tribe", "version", "pop_2014", "pop_2024"]
wide["growth"] = (wide.pop_2024 / wide.pop_2014 - 1) * 100

# Each report has its own typical growth: the median of that report
wide["vs_typical"] = wide.growth - wide.groupby("version").growth.transform("median")
```

### Bar chart of growth

Growth maps to the *length* of a bar, which starts at zero. Sorting the
tribes by growth puts the tribes that shrank at the bottom and the fastest
growers at the top. The dashed line marks the median growth, so you can see
how far each bar is from typical.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: alt_bars
provisional = wide[wide.version == "bad"].sort_values("growth")
provisional = provisional.assign(
    tribe=pd.Categorical(provisional.tribe.astype(str), categories=provisional.tribe.astype(str))
)
median_growth = provisional.growth.median()

(
    ggplot(provisional, aes(x="tribe", y="growth"))
    + geom_col()
    + annotate("hline", yintercept=median_growth, linetype="dashed")
    + annotate("text", label="median", x=1, y=median_growth, ha="left")
    + coord_flip()
    + labs(y="Growth, 2014 to 2024 (%)")
)
```

### Box plot of growth

A box plot drops the tribes' identities and shows only the *distribution* of
growth in each report. The box holds the middle half of the tribes. A point
far outside it is an outlier. Here we label them.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: alt_box
outliers = wide[wide.vs_typical.abs() > 15]

(
    ggplot(wide, aes(x="version", y="growth"))
    + geom_boxplot(outlier_alpha=0)
    + geom_point()
    + geom_text(aes(label="tribe"), data=outliers, ha="left", nudge_x=0.08, size=8)
    + labs(y="Growth, 2014 to 2024 (%)")
)
```

### Lollipop chart of growth

Growth maps to position along a shared axis, with a stem to anchor each
point at zero. Facets compare the provisional and corrected figures.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: alt_lollipop
(
    ggplot(wide, aes(x="growth", y="tribe"))
    + geom_segment(aes(x=0, xend="growth", yend="tribe"), color="grey")
    + geom_point()
    + facet_wrap("version")
    + labs(x="Growth, 2014 to 2024 (%)")
)
```

### Indexed slope chart

Year maps to x position and each tribe is one line, so the *slope* carries
the change. To compare tribes of different sizes on a linear axis, each
tribe's 2014 population is set to 1. A line that ends at 2 doubled and
a line that ends below 1 shrank.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: alt_index
provisional = wide[wide.version == "bad"]
index = provisional.melt(
    id_vars=["tribe", "growth", "vs_typical"],
    value_vars=["pop_2014", "pop_2024"],
    var_name="year",
    value_name="population",
).assign(
    year=lambda d: d.year.str[-4:],
    population=lambda d: d.population / d.groupby("tribe").population.transform("first"),
    shrank=lambda d: d.growth < 0,
)

(
    ggplot(index, aes(x="year", y="population", group="tribe", color="shrank"))
    + geom_line()
    + geom_point()
    + geom_text(
        aes(label="tribe"),
        data=index[(index.year == "2024") & (index.vs_typical.abs() > 15)],
        ha="left",
        nudge_x=0.05,
        size=8,
    )
    + annotate("hline", yintercept=1)
    + annotate("text", label="No Growth", x=float("inf"), y=1, va="bottom", ha="right", size=8)
    + scale_x_discrete(expand=(0.05, 0, 0.4, 0))
    + labs(y="Population (2014 = 1)")
    + theme(legend_position="none")
)
```

Every one of these plots could have caught the error. They differ in what
they ask the reader to judge: a length, a distance from the box, a position
along a shared axis or a slope.
